page9_img_1.png.title: Per-bug annotation token and time tax: Flow vs TypeScript
page9_img_1.png.description: A two-row summary table comparing the per-bug annotation "token tax" and "time tax" for Flow and TypeScript (seconds). Columns report Token Tax (Mean, Median) and Time Tax in seconds (Mean, Median). Flow shows a token-tax mean of 1.7 and median of 2 tokens, with a time-tax mean of 231.4 s and median of 133 s; TypeScript shows a token-tax mean of 2.4 and median of 2 tokens, with a time-tax mean of 306.8 s and median of 262 s. These values are the authors’ under-approximation of the annotation effort required to make a bug trigger a type error (measured only for bugs detected by either system).

page3_img_2.png.title: Automatic matching of commits and bug reports to produce linked fix candidates
page3_img_2.png.description: A simple flowchart showing how the study automatically finds candidate bug-fixing commits by cross-referencing version-control and issue-tracker data. The diagram depicts two inputs — ‘Commit Logs’ and the issue tracker — with boxes that extract issue numbers from commit messages and extract commit SHAs from issue reports; both streams feed into a central repository labeled “Linked Fix Candidates.” As described in the paper, these matches are cross-checked to produce triples (candidate commit SHA, parent SHA, bug-report ID) that are later manually validated to build the corpus of fixes.

page4_img_table_1.png.title: Project and fix size statistics (LOC)
page4_img_table_1.png.description: Two-row table reporting LOC (lines of code) summary statistics (Max, Min, Mean, Median) for repository projects and for individual fixes. Projects (398 in the corpus) range from 32 to 1,144,440 LOC with a mean of 18,117.9 and a median of 1,736, indicating a highly skewed size distribution across repositories. Fixes range from 1 to 270 LOC with a mean of 16.2 and a median of 6, consistent with the paper’s observation that typical bug-fixing commits modify only a few lines (about 48% touch five or fewer LOC).

page4_img_fig_1.png.title: Workflow for identifying and type‑checking historical JavaScript bug fixes
page4_img_fig_1.png.description: A left-to-right pipeline diagram showing the study’s workflow: GitHub (icon) supplies Projects, Issues, and Commit Logs into a “Link Identification” step that matches issue IDs and commit SHAs to produce candidate fixes. Candidates are passed to a human ‘Filter’ (person icon) to select buggy program versions, then to a human ‘Annotate’ step where type annotations are added, producing annotated programs. Those annotated programs go into a “Type Checking” box (Flow/TypeScript) whose outcome (cylinder) is stored as Detectable Bugs. This diagram summarizes Procedure 1 in the paper and the data flow that produced the corpus of 400 sampled bugs later analyzed (resulting in ≈60 bugs detectable by each checker, about a 15% detection rate).

page3_img_1.png.title: Venn diagram of ts-detectable and patched public bugs
page3_img_1.png.description: A Venn-style schematic that situates the study’s targets: the outer area represents all bugs, a nested region denotes public bugs, and a hatched circle inside that denotes patched (fixed) public bugs. A separate circle labeled “ts-detectable bugs” overlaps the patched-public-bugs circle; the solid blue overlap marks the subset of fixed public bugs that become type-check errors after adding consistent annotations (i.e., bugs a static type system could have flagged). The hatched portion of the patched-public-bugs circle outside the blue area represents fixed public bugs that the type systems would not detect under the experiment’s annotation model. The experiment quantifies the size of that blue overlap (Equation 1) and reports that Flow and TypeScript each detect about 15% of public bugs.

page6_img_1.png.title: Venn diagram of Flow- and TypeScript-detectable bugs
page6_img_1.png.description: A two-circle Venn diagram comparing which public bugs are detected by Flow versus TypeScript. Out of the 400 assessed bugs, Flow and TypeScript each detect 60 bugs; the diagram shows an intersection of 57 bugs detected by both tools, with 3 bugs unique to Flow and 3 unique to TypeScript (63 distinct detectable bugs total). The figure supports the paper’s claim that the two type systems largely overlap in the bugs they can detect (overall detection rate ≈15%).

page8_img_1.png.title: Histogram of undetectable public bugs by category
page8_img_1.png.description: Bar chart reporting the categories of public bugs that were undetectable by both Flow and TypeScript. Of the 400 bugs in the corpus, 63 were detected by at least one system, leaving 337 undetectable cases; the chart shows that SpecError is dominant with 186 occurrences (~55% of undetectable bugs). StringError is the second-largest category, followed by BranchError, PredError, UIError and RegExError with noticeably smaller counts, while APIError, SyntaxError, RangeError and ResError are rare. The paper highlights that errors implementing the specification (SpecError plus related logic categories such as BranchError and PredError) together make up roughly 78% of the undetectable bugs.
